extracted.intended_audience: readers of maritime history; historians; shipping and sailing enthusiasts
extracted.subtask_description: Chronological, descriptive account of clipper and sailing-ship passages between the United Kingdom and Australia (Melbourne/Sydney) in the late 19th century, with tables of voyage dates/durations and narrative commentary on ship performance, incidents, and port practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passage duration (notability threshold: under 80 days)
rubrics_metrics.description: Passages to Sydney or Melbourne completed in fewer than 80 days are singled out and tabulated as noteworthy (headings: 'PASSAGES UNDER 80 DAYS TO MELBOURNE IN 1876', 'PASSAGES TO SYDNEY UNDER 80 DAYS IN 1877', etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page repeatedly uses 'under 80 days' as a benchmark of a 'crack' or notable passage; tables record departure, equator, Cape meridian, Otway/S.W. Cape, arrival and 'Days Out'. Example: many entries are presented because they were under 80 days.

rubrics_metrics.name: Average passage time
rubrics_metrics.description: Average days over a series of voyages is used to compare ships (e.g., 'Taking the average of 16 outward passages ... _Brilliant’s_ record to be 85 days, her rival _Pericles_ had an average of 84 days').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Averages over multiple voyages are treated as an indicator of a ship's consistent performance rather than single fast runs; useful when comparing rival ships or captains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best week’s work / 24-hour run (distance metrics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mileage logged over defined periods ('best week’s work', 'best 24 hour’s run') used to demonstrate a ship's speed and capability (e.g., 'her best week’s work was 1860 miles, and her best 24 hour’s run...336 miles').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Day/week mileage figures (e.g., runs of 300–350 miles per day, week totals over 2000 miles) are cited as concrete measures of performance and as evidence when assessing a ship or voyage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maiden passage and single-voyage exceptional runs
rubrics_metrics.description: A ship's maiden voyage or single exceptional passages are noted as markers of potential or reputation (e.g., '_Brilliant_ on her maiden passage went out to Sydney in 78 days', 'On her maiden passage _Brilliant_ ... three consecutive runs of 340, 345 and 338 miles').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maiden passages and spectacular single runs are highlighted, but the narrative also cautions that single voyages may not equal sustained superiority (hence use with averages).

rubrics_metrics.name: Loading condition / cargo effect on speed
rubrics_metrics.description: The ship's loading (light load line vs loaded deep with cargo or emigrants) is used to explain varying performance: 'Pericles usually took emigrants out, Brilliant being loaded deep with general cargo; ... Pericles with her light load line generally won the hat going out, but the Brilliant was always very hard to beat on the homeward run.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observers attribute differences in outbound vs homeward performance to load; evaluators should consider cargo and load_line when judging voyage times.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hull form / ship lines (sharp-ended vs fuller-bodied)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ship design—'sharp-ended' versus 'fuller' hulls—is used as a qualitative criterion for speed or capacity: e.g., 'Loch Ryan ... was not as sharp-ended as her predecessors and was more of a carrier', '_Sophocles_ ... given a fuller body ... meant to be an economical carrier rather than a record breaker.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hull form indicates intended role (speed vs cargo capacity) and explains why some vessels rarely achieve record passages despite size.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seaworthiness and safety (overloading and structural damage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Safety considerations such as being 'too deeply loaded for safety' or sustaining structural damage in heavy weather are used to critique voyage and ship handling (e.g., 'Patriarch ... lost 9 feet of her taffrail and three stanchions over the side' and 'Thessalus ... on her arrival critics declared that she was too deeply loaded for safety').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Passage performance must be balanced against safety; 'fast' passages achieved at the cost of unsafe loading or damage are pointed out as problematic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Captain skill and seamanship record
rubrics_metrics.description: The professional competence of a captain is treated as an evaluative criterion—examples include Captain Stuart's boast 'he had never lost a man or a mast overboard' and accounts of captains 'driving' ships for performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long-term records of safe command, crew retention, and successful management of ships across many voyages are used to assess captaincy and contribute to a ship's reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causes of wrecks and navigation errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Accounts of wrecks cite specific causal factors—mistaking lights, being 'held up' by calms or squalls, overrun distance, and cliffs blocking visibility (e.g., 'master mistook the Great Castle Head lights', 'overran her distance and was wrecked on Kangaroo Island').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accidents are analyzed in terms of navigational decisions and environmental conditions; evaluators note these causes when judging the competence of officers or safety of routes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Port practices and berth allocation etiquette (legal/procedural standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Port arrangements and legal norms (booking order for berths; 'free berth' system) determine acceptable conduct—Captain Fimister's act of 'jumping _Patriarch's_ loading berth' led to official action and a fine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adherence to harbour rules and booking procedures is a procedural standard; violating them risks fines and official removal regardless of commercial advantage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Market conditions influence on routing and employment
rubrics_metrics.description: Freight market conditions affect whether ships pursue record runs or seek alternative trades: 'It was a time of depressed freights and ships found themselves seeking cargoes in other than their regular trades.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Voyage selection and apparent performance must be interpreted in the context of freight markets; poor freights can lead to atypical routes or poorer voyage records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of voyage logs/abstract logs as authoritative evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Detailed log extracts (positions, courses, daily distances, winds) are presented as primary evidence of performance (e.g., 'ABSTRACT LOG OF _CIMBA_ FROM CALLAO TO IQUIQUE' with daily lat/long/course/dist/wind).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Log entries and abstracts are treated as the factual basis for mileage claims and performance assessments; they are the recommended evidence when asserting records or runs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disposition of ships as an indicator of commercial lifecycle
rubrics_metrics.description: Sale, change of registry, repurposing (e.g., training ship, sale to Norwegians, broken up) are used to indicate a ship's commercial viability or end of career (e.g., '_Loch Ryan_ ... bought by the Victorian Government and turned into a boys’ training ship', 'Thompson’s sold _Pericles_ to the Norwegians in 1904').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Changes in ownership, role, or flag are reported as outcomes reflecting market conditions, ship condition, or obsolescence and can be used to evaluate a ship's long-term success.
